issues.legal_issue: An executive delegate cannot use an exemption power to make a permanent change that alters the essential policy of the rent-control legislation or effectively removes its protection for most tenancies.
material_facts: An executive authority issued a notification exempting buildings and rented land with monthly rent above a specified threshold from the rent-control legislation, without limiting the exemption to a set period.
The notification was issued to advance a housing-policy approach that contemplated changes to rent-control laws through legislation.
The threshold was adopted without adequate collection or assessment of relevant data, including prevailing rents and economic changes.
The exemption applied broadly and had a permanent effect, removing statutory protection from a substantial section of tenants.
issues.conclusion: The notification was invalid because the executive authority exceeded its delegated power by making a permanent, broad change contrary to the legislation’s policy; the judgments upholding the notification were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, an exemption notification must remain within the Act’s legislative policy and cannot efface the Act or alter its essential features. The exemption power is reviewable, and a permanent change in legislative policy must be made by the legislature, not by an executive delegate. The Court relied on P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, B.K. Industries v. Union of India, Hindustan Lever v. Hindustan Lever Mazdoor Sabha, Clariant International v. SEBI, D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, and Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

rule.if: challenge_to_executive_exemption and permanent_exemption and policy_change_requires_legislation and threshold_set_without_adequate_data and most_tenancies_lost_protection

predicates.challenge_to_executive_exemption: A party challenged an executive notification granting an exemption from statutory protections.
predicates.permanent_exemption: The exemption was not limited to a defined period and therefore had a lasting effect.
predicates.policy_change_requires_legislation: The executive used the exemption to implement a change in policy that called for alteration of the governing law by the legislature.
predicates.threshold_set_without_adequate_data: The executive selected the exemption threshold without adequately assessing relevant facts such as prevailing rents and changed economic conditions.
predicates.most_tenancies_lost_protection: The exemption removed statutory protection from a substantial section of tenancies.

issues.definition: When an executive exemption is challenged, it is permanent, implements a policy change reserved for legislation, rests on an inadequately assessed threshold, and removes protection from most tenancies, the exemption is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Rental value may be used as a basis for distinguishing tenanted premises for an exemption from rent-control protection.
material_facts: The challenged notification distinguished premises according to the monthly rent they fetched.
The statutory definition of a building included a building or part of a building let for any purpose.
The Court accepted that the rent of a tenanted building could be relevant to classifying premises, while finding the particular threshold unsupported and the notification invalid for other reasons.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that a rent-based criterion is inherently unlawful; rental value may be a relevant basis for classification, although the particular threshold in this case was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: A classification based on rental value is not invalid merely because it uses rent as its criterion, provided the classification has a rational relationship to its purpose and remains within the governing law. The Court referred to the definition of “building” in Section 2(a) and the exemption power in Section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, and considered S. Kandaswamy Chettiar v. State of Tamil Nadu, D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, and Delhi Cloth & General Mills v. S. Paramjit Singh.

predicates.challenge_to_rent_based_exemption: A party challenged an exemption that distinguished rented premises according to the rent they fetched.
predicates.premises_have_different_rental_values: The rented premises in the relevant class had differing rental values.

issues.definition: When an exemption based on rental value is challenged and premises have differing rental values, rental value may be used as a classification basis.

issues.legal_issue: An executive notification granting an exemption from the operation of a statute is subordinate legislation subject to judicial review.
material_facts: The executive authority issued a notification determining that the rent-control legislation would not apply to a class of premises.
The respondents argued that the notification was conditional legislation rather than delegated legislation.
The Court held that the notification exercised delegated rule-making power because it exempted a class from the application of the statute.
issues.conclusion: The notification was delegated legislation, not conditional legislation, and was subject to judicial review.
issues.legal_principle: Conditional legislation leaves to the executive the determination of when or where a complete legislative rule will take effect; delegated legislation authorizes the executive to make rules or otherwise exercise legislative power within statutory limits. A notification granting exemption from a statute’s operation is delegated legislation. The Court relied on Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) v. Union of India, M.P. High Court Bar Association v. Union of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Sabanayagam, and Orient Paper and Industries v. State of Orissa.

predicates.challenge_to_exemption_notification: A party challenged an executive notification concerning whether a statute applied to a class of cases or persons.
predicates.executive_decides_statutory_protection_f: The executive determined that statutory protections would not apply to a defined class.

issues.definition: When a challenged notification lets the executive determine that statutory protection will not apply to a class, the notification is delegated legislation subject to judicial review.

issues.legal_issue: A delegated exemption from rent-control protection is reviewable for inconsistency with legislative policy, discrimination, reliance on irrelevant grounds, or bad faith.
material_facts: Tenants challenged an executive exemption notification under the rent-control legislation.
The notification removed protections against eviction and rent increases for the class of premises it covered.
The Court examined whether the exemption remained within the legislation’s purpose and whether the executive had considered relevant facts.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the exemption notification was subject to judicial review and that its validity had to be assessed against the legislation’s policy and the relevant grounds for exercising the exemption power.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of delegated legislation is available for inconsistency with the enabling Act or the Constitution. For an exemption power, review is wider and includes whether the exemption is discriminatory, based on grounds germane to the Act’s policy and purpose, or made in bad faith. The Court relied on P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India, and the principles in Bombay Dyeing & Manufacturing Co. v. Bombay Environmental Action Group.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_exemption: A party challenged an exemption made by an executive authority exercising power delegated by legislation.
predicates.exemption_affects_statutory_protection: The exemption altered whether a class received protections under the statute.

issues.definition: When a challenged delegated exemption affects statutory protection, its validity is subject to judicial review.
